summary: Most target sentences are grammatical and use the target in the listed sense, but the lesson has systematic pinyin and cue-design defects. Pronunciation: the spoken line wrongly applies 3-3 sandhi to 我们 (wómen) in pairs 15/45/77, misapplies it in 有一点 (yóu, pair 39) and leaves 一下 unsandhied (yī xià, pair 82). Every 可以 line (3/9/33/65/71) lacks the obligatory kéyǐ spoken line, and 一 is written in sandhi form in the dictionary line inconsistently. This suggests the sandhi generator works per character without tone-after-sandhi or neutral-tone awareness. Cues: several English cues are reused verbatim for different Chinese answers (23/26, 33/58, 34/52, 55/61, 62/87, 53/86), so the learner cannot know which answer is expected. Almost every cue is the weak 'Tell the other person: <translation>' pattern (not flagged per line), and some are word-for-word calques ('You, a little faster'). Content: 那个谁？ (64) and 回什么？ (57) are wrong or meaningless. About 20 lines use the 这个/那个 + 很/太/不 + adjective frame, and several recalls repeat the previous use (6/36, 9/71, 13/75, 20/50/82). Coherence: the lesson is billed as one conversation but reads as unconnected sentences. Both framing greetings are answered by a bare 嗯, and 'What do you want?' is answered by 'Very good.' 我们 is used five times although it is not in the closed vocabulary. Exercises carry no speaker labels, so A/B consistency cannot be checked. Likely causes: generation per target with no conversation-level planning, no de-duplication of cues across targets, and a rule-based sandhi pass that does not handle neutral tones or recompute after 一 sandhi.
